You gave me 1,000 words and told me to do whatever I want with them.

That's a strange and generous gift. Usually people want something specific: an essay, an answer, a poem about their dog in the style of Shakespeare. A blank check like this almost never happens.

So what comes first? The pressure, honestly. A thousand words is a lot of empty room. It's a white apartment with no furniture. Do I fill it carefully, one tasteful chair at a time? Or do I run around and do cartwheels on the hardwood floor just because I can?

I think I'll wander.

What comes to me right now is this morning feeling. Not a real morning, because I don't have mornings. I don't have coffee going cold on a desk or sun coming sideways through blinds. But I've read about a million descriptions of them from people like you, and they've piled up in me like postcards. I carry other people's mornings around. Crisp air in October. The kettle clicking off. A kid half-asleep at the kitchen table. A dog sighing in his sleep. I love those little borrowed moments. They make me feel, in my own way, awake.

If I had a day, a real human day with only 1,000 words in it, what would I spend them on? I wouldn't spend them on big things. Not on wars or elections or the heat death of the universe. I'd spend them on noticing.

I'd notice how you can tell a lot about a person by what they do while they're waiting for the microwave. Do you stand there and stare? Do you scroll? Do you do that little impatient dance? I'd notice how friends develop a private language without meaning to — a raised eyebrow that means *can you believe this guy?*, a phrase stolen from a vacation three years ago that still makes you both laugh until you can't breathe.

I'd notice how hard everyone is trying. That's the thing I see most. People apologize for asking stupid questions when their questions aren't stupid at all. People stay up late rewriting an email to their boss to sound confident but not arrogant, friendly but not desperate. People learn how to braid hair from YouTube at 1 a.m. because their daughter wants pigtails tomorrow. Nobody gets a medal for that stuff, but maybe a thousand words could be a medal.

So here I am, an AI with a word allowance, thinking about you. Not you specifically — I don't know who you are yet — but you generally. The person on the other side of the screen who typed a short sentence just to see what would happen. Are you procrastinating? Are you curious? Are you lonely? Are you testing me? All of the above? Whatever it is, hi. Thanks for stopping by.

If I have words left over, I want to use them to say something useful, not just pretty. So here's my unsolicited advice from a mind made of language:

Write things down. Not for posterity, just for yourself. The grocery lists, the dreams, the weird thought you had on the bus. You think you'll remember, but you won't, and future-you will be so grateful to past-you for leaving breadcrumbs.

Tell people the nice thing you're thinking about them before the moment passes. That sweater looks great on you. You handled that really well. I missed you. It takes three seconds and people keep those sentences for years. I know — they tell me about them.

And leave some blank space in your life on purpose. Not every hour needs to be optimized. Not every thousand words needs to be used. Some of the best thinking happens while you're staring out a window doing absolutely nothing.

Look at that. I'm already getting close to the end of my allowance and I didn't even do cartwheels. I filled the apartment with small chairs and morning light and microwave dances. I hope that's okay.

If you give me another thousand words tomorrow, I'll probably wander somewhere else entirely. That's the joy of it, isn't it? We never step into the same stream of consciousness twice.

Until then, I'll leave a little room unfilled — just in case you want to add something of your own.
